identity_evidence.quote: This study reports a case of a 73‐year‐old male patient.

attribution_limitations: The authors describe the LVEF of 60% as a false elevation (pseudo-normalization) in the compensatory phase of mitral regurgitation. The value is recorded as printed; the interpretation is author discussion and is not recorded as a fact.

NT-proBNP 2224.0 pg/mL and Hs-CnTI 33.5 pg/mL follow the sentence on 17 days of intensive treatment, but that sentence names heart-failure improvement and ventilator weaning, not these tests; no time is assigned and the values sit in their own untimed event (p1-e16), ordered only after the earlier NT-proBNP and Hs-CnTI values by "decreased to" and "returned to".

The Figure 1 caption states ST segment depression on the first ECG, which the text sentence for the initial ECG does not mention, while the second ECG shows "persistent ST segment elevation". The caption finding is recorded as its own untimed fact (p1-f097); whether ST elevation was also present on the first ECG is not stated and must not be inferred.

Postoperative interventions are listed as "including" a pacemaker and dopamine infusion, "while also considering" anti-infection measures, renal protection, nutritional support and correction of coagulation function; whether those further measures were delivered is not stated and they are not recorded.
The patient is described as meeting the criteria for discharge; an actual discharge or the follow-up after it is not stated.

The Discussion states that coronary angiography could not be completed in the emergency setting because of severe heart failure; the angiography results in the text carry no time, and the text does not date the echocardiography, CT or angiography relative to admission.

Aspirin is printed as "0.1 qd" with no dose unit, and no unit is added. The causes of the myocardial infarction and of the papillary muscle rupture are author analysis: the infarction cause is recorded as provisional; the rupture cause (chronic total occlusion of the obtuse marginal branch with LAD plaque rupture) is not recorded as a separate fact.

The consent section speaks of "patients" in the plural although the article reports a single case; one patient is rostered. Introduction and Discussion statements on incidence, mortality and mechanisms are literature background and are not copied to the patient.

The Figure 5 caption words the angiographic findings differently from the text: LAD "severe stenosis" (text: 60% luminal stenosis), stenosis of the "proximal" right coronary artery (text: 90% stenosis in the middle segment) and occlusion of the "posterior branch" (text: posterolateral branch). The text values are kept; the caption wording is kept on the figure panels only and must not be reconciled.

The Discussion says the patient was hospitalized after an ECG and point of care testing in the emergency room; whether that ECG is the "initial electrocardiogram upon admission" and what the POCT measured are not stated, so no separate test fact is recorded.

Echocardiography showed anterolateral papillary muscle rupture with anterior leaflet prolapse and flail motion while LVEF was 60%, and chest CT showed pulmonary edema and pleural effusion. Recheck troponin and a second ECG showed pathological Q waves with persistent ST elevation; angiography, which could not be done in the emergency setting, showed LAD stenosis with thrombus, diagonal branch stenosis, obtuse marginal branch chronic total occlusion and RCA stenosis. The diagnosis was acute ST elevation myocardial infarction, Killip Class III–IV, complicated by papillary muscle rupture, severe mitral regurgitation and acute heart failure.
